# Introduction


# Naive set theory

We begin with two primitive informal notions: **objects** and **sets**.
Roughly speaking, a set is a collection of objects, and the most basic question we can ask is whether a given object belongs to a given set.
If the object $x$ belongs to the set $A$, we write
$$
x\in A,
$$
and if it does not belong to $A$, we write
$$
x\notin A.
$$
An intuitive example is given by the natural numbers
$$
\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,3,\dots\},
$$
but at this stage this should be understood only informally.

This informal viewpoint is useful, but also delicate.
If one tries to take the notion of set completely literally and declare that every possible collection of objects is automatically a set, contradictions appear.
The most famous one is **Russell's paradox**, which can be explained through the **barber's paradox**: imagine a barber who shaves exactly those people in a village who do not shave themselves.
Does the barber shave himself?
If he does, then by definition he should not; if he does not, then by definition he should.
The set-theoretic paradox has the same logical flavour and warns us that foundations must be handled with care.
Taking that issue seriously would force us into a long discussion on logic and the foundations of mathematics, which is far beyond the scope of this course.
So we adopt a pragmatic axiomatic point of view.

In these notes, we work with **objects** and **sets**, and we regard every set as an object.
However, not every object is automatically considered to be a set.
For instance, the number $3$ is an object, while the singleton $\{3\}$ is a set and therefore also an object.
This is sometimes called an **impure** point of view.
In **pure set theory**, by contrast, everything is ultimately regarded as a set.
We will occasionally keep that picture in mind, following the discussion in Tao's *Analysis I*, but we will not need to push it very far.

::: {.callout-warning title="Numbers Will Be Treated Informally"}

::: {#wrn-numbers-treated-informally}

We will **not** build the natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, or real numbers from scratch in this course.
Doing so carefully would require a substantial amount of additional foundational material.
Instead, we rely on the intuitive understanding we already have of
$$
\mathbb{N},\qquad \mathbb{Z},\qquad \mathbb{Q},\qquad \mathbb{R},
$$
and we will explicitly point out the properties and subtleties of these number systems whenever they become relevant.

In particular, when we speak about the natural numbers below, we are not trying to derive them from first principles.
We merely record the basic existence assumption that allows us to use them in the rest of the course.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Equality of Sets"}

::: {#def-equality-of-sets}

Two sets $A$ and $B$ are said to be **equal** if they have exactly the same elements, that is, if for every object $x$ one has
$$
x\in A \Longleftrightarrow x\in B.
$$
Thus, when dealing with sets, what matters is not the order in which the elements are written, nor how many times they are listed, but only which objects belong to the set.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Axiom 3.1: Sets Are Objects"}

::: {#axm-sets-are-objects}

Every set is an object.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Axiom 3.2: Empty Set"}

::: {#axm-empty-set}

There exists a set with no elements, called the **empty set** and denoted by
$$
\emptyset=\{\}.
$$

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Axiom 3.3: Singleton Sets"}

::: {#axm-singleton-set}

If $x$ is an object, then there exists a set whose only element is $x$.
This set is called the **singleton** associated with $x$ and is denoted by
$$
\{x\}.
$$

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Axiom 3.4: Pair Sets"}

::: {#axm-pair-set}

If $x$ and $y$ are objects, then there exists a set whose elements are exactly $x$ and $y$.
This set is denoted by
$$
\{x,y\}.
$$
If $x=y$, this is just the singleton $\{x\}$.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Axiom 3.5: Pairwise Union"}

::: {#axm-pairwise-union}

If $A$ and $B$ are sets, then there exists a set whose elements are precisely those objects that belong to $A$ or to $B$.
This set is called the **union** of $A$ and $B$ and is denoted by
$$
A\cup B.
$$

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Axiom 3.6: Specification"}

::: {#axm-specification}

Let $A$ be a set, and let $P(x)$ be a property referring to objects $x$.
Then there exists a set consisting of exactly those elements of $A$ for which $P(x)$ is true.
We denote it by
$$
\{x\in A \,:\, P(x)\}.
$$
This is the basic operation that allows us to carve out subsets from sets that already exist.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Axiom 3.7: Replacement"}

::: {#axm-replacement}

Let $A$ be a set, and suppose that to each element $x\in A$ we assign a unique object $f(x)$.
Then the collection of all such outputs
$$
\{f(x)\,:\, x\in A\}
$$
is again a set.

This axiom says that if we start with a set and systematically replace each of its elements by another object, the resulting collection is still a set.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Axiom 3.8: Natural Numbers"}

::: {#axm-natural-numbers}

There exists a set $\mathbb{N}$ whose elements are called the **natural numbers**, together with a distinguished element $0\in\mathbb{N}$ and a successor operation
$$
n\mapsto n+1
$$
which sends each natural number to another natural number.

We will not discuss the formal [Peano axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_axioms) here, nor will we attempt to construct the integers, rationals, or reals from $\mathbb{N}$.
Instead, we use the familiar intuitive number systems and record explicitly whatever algebraic or order-theoretic properties we need later on.

:::

:::

The previous axioms are enough for the level of set theory we need in this course.
In particular, we deliberately stop here and do **not** pursue the more delicate axioms connected with Russell-type paradoxes.

::: {.callout-note title="Basic Set Operations"}

::: {#def-basic-set-operations}

Let $A,B,X$ be sets.
We write
$$
A\subseteq X
$$
if every element of $A$ is also an element of $X$.

The **intersection** of $A$ and $B$ is the set
$$
A\cap B:=\{x\in A \,:\, x\in B\}.
$$

The **difference** of $A$ and $B$ is the set
$$
A\setminus B:=\{x\in A \,:\, x\notin B\}.
$$

If $A\subseteq X$, the **complement** of $A$ in $X$ is the set
$$
X\setminus A=\{x\in X \,:\, x\notin A\}.
$$
When a reference set $X$ is understood from the context, one often writes this complement as $A^{c}$.

For two sets $A$ and $B$, their **Cartesian product** is the set
$$
A\times B:=\{(a,b)\,:\, a\in A,\ b\in B\}.
$$
Here $(a,b)$ denotes the ordered pair formed by $a$ and $b$; we treat ordered pairs as familiar objects without trying to construct them from sets.

More generally, if $A_{1},\dots,A_{n}$ are sets, we define their **finite Cartesian product** by
$$
\prod_{j=1}^{n}A_{j}
:=
\left\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\,:\, x_{j}\in A_{j}\ \mbox{ for every } j=1,\dots,n\right\}.
$$

:::

:::


# Functions



::: {.callout-warning title="How we will write functions"}

::: {#rem-how-we-write-functions}

Sometimes, we may be forced to talk about the function $f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y$ given by $f(x)=y$ multiple times when proving a theorem, solving an exercise, or discussing an idea.
To avoid an absurd amount of notationally-heavy repetitions, once the domain, the input space, the output  space, and the explicit rule $f(x)=y$ have been clearly defined as above, we will often write just $f(x)=y$, or even just $f$, for the rest of the proof of the theorem, or of the exercise, or of the discussion.

Moreover, sometimes we may be introducing a subset $D\subseteq X$, and later introduce a function having $D$ as domain. 
In this case, we often writes $f\colon D\rightarrow Y$ given by $f(x)=y$ omitting the input space since it is clear from the context.

:::

# Real numbers

We need to introduce various types of intervals. These objects help in formalizing the way $x$ approaches $x_{0}$.

::: {.callout-note title="Open and closed intervals"}

::: {#def-open-closed-intervals} 
 
Let $a<b\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\cup\{-\infty\}$.
Here and throughout, inequalities involving $\pm\infty$ use the usual order on the extended real line.
We define the **open interval** $(a,b)$ as the subset of $\mathbb{R}$ given by
$$
(a,b):= \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a< x < b \}.
$$ {#eq-open-interval}
If either $a=-\infty$ or $b=+\infty$, the interval is said to be **unbounded**.

When $a\neq-\infty$ and $b\neq+\infty$, we define the closed interval $[a,b]$ as
$$
[a,b]:= \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a\leq x \leq b \}.
$$

Intuitively speaking, the interval $(a,b)$ is _open_ because its boundary points **are not** part of it, while $[a,b]$ is _closed_ because its boundary points **are** part of it.

:::

:::

Not all intervals are either open or closed. For instance, when $a\neq-\infty$, we can define the interval $[a,b)$ as
$$
[a,b) := \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a\leq x < b\},
$$
while, when $b\neq+\infty$, we can define the interval $(a,b]$ as
$$
(a,b] := \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a < x \leq b\}, 
$$
and it's clear that these interval are neither open nor closed in the sense of @def-open-closed-intervals




In the following, it will be useful to also consider the **symmetric open interval**
$$
I_{x_{0},\varepsilon}\equiv(x_{0}-\varepsilon, x_{0}+\varepsilon)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad x_{0}-\varepsilon < x < x_{0} + \varepsilon\}
$$
centered at $x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ with length $2\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. It is not hard to see that if $x\in I_{x_{0},\varepsilon}$, then either $x-x_{0}< \varepsilon$  or $x_{0} - x <\varepsilon$. It then follows that $|x-x_{0}|<\varepsilon$, so that
$$ 
I_{x_{0},\varepsilon}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,| \quad d(x_{0},x)<\varepsilon\}. 
$$
Therefore, the symmetric open intervals of $\mathbb{R}$ may be determined through the distance function.



::: {.callout-note title="Accumulation point"}

::: {#def-accumulation-point}

A point $x_{0}\in \mathbb{R}$ is said to be a **left accumulation point** for the subset $D$ if for every $r>0$ there exists $x\in D$ such that
$$
x_0-r<x<x_0.
$$
A point $x_{0}\in \mathbb{R}$ is said to be a **right accumulation point** for $D$ if for every $r>0$ there exists $x\in D$ such that
$$
x_0<x<x_0+r.
$$

A point which is a left (right) accumulation point but not a right (left) accumulation point is called a **strict left accumulation point** (**strict right accumulation point**). 

A point $x_0\in\mathbb{R}$ is said to be an **accumulation point** for $D$ if for every $r>0$ there exists $x\in D$ with $x\neq x_0$ such that
$$
|x-x_0|<r,
$$ 
which means it is both a left and right accumulation point.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Isolated point"}

::: {#def-isolated-point}

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $x_{0}\in D$.
We say that $x_{0}$ is an **isolated point** of $D$ if there exists $r>0$ such that
$$
D\cap(x_{0}-r,x_{0}+r)=\{x_{0}\}.
$$

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Accumulation at infinity"}

::: {#def-accumulation-point-at-infinity}

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}$.
We say that $+\infty$ is a **right accumulation point** for $D$ if for every $R>0$ there exists $x\in D$ such that
$$
x>R.
$$
We say that $-\infty$ is a **left accumulation point** for $D$ if for every $R>0$ there exists $x\in D$ such that
$$
x<-R.
$$

:::

:::
